story.headline: US envoy meets Putin, Russia frees Hubbard
story.summary: Witkoff met Putin in St Petersburg a day after talks with Zelensky in Oslo.
story.display_body: US envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday 21 October, and Putin announced during the talks that Russia was releasing jailed American Stephen Hubbard. This was the ninth in-person meeting between the two, according to DW, and it came a day after Witkoff's talks with Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo on Tuesday 20 October. The prime ministers of Norway and Finland and representatives of the EU and NATO also attended in Oslo; US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called those talks "positive" and said Witkoff would take "those ideas" to the Russian side. After Oslo, Zelensky said "very, very important" US intelligence sharing had been restored. Hubbard was captured in Ukraine and sentenced in 2024, at a closed trial, to seven years on mercenary charges he denies. DW reports that Putin also proposed discussing the restoration of US–Russian ties and a possible meeting with Donald Trump in Beijing. A separate dispute is still open: the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing US officials, that Elon Musk himself ordered the slowdown of SpaceX's satellite service for Ukraine; Rubio says the decision lies with the company, while Musk says only the US military and president can make it.
story.why: the talks follow Trump's open clash with Zelensky earlier this week, and Kyiv's access to US intelligence and satellite links now sits alongside the peace terms being discussed.

story.headline: Drone strike on Abyei market kills 153
story.summary: A drone strike on Amiet Market in disputed Abyei killed at least 153 people; South Sudan blames Sudan's army.
story.display_body: A drone strike on Amiet Market in the disputed Abyei region between Sudan and South Sudan on Monday 19 October killed at least 153 people, the region's caretaker information minister said on Tuesday 20 October. Yohanna Akol Ngor had given a toll of 73 the day before. He said some bodies had been burned to ashes and that around 8,000 people had been displaced. The drone hit a fuel depot, which caused a fire that was still burning on Tuesday. South Sudan's foreign ministry blamed Sudan's army and summoned Sudan's ambassador; neither it nor Abyei officials gave evidence. A senior Sudanese officer, speaking anonymously to AP, said the army targeted fuel tankers headed for the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and that the dead were RSF members and smugglers. UN spokesman Stéphane Dujarric said dozens of civilians, including women and children, were killed, without naming who carried out the strike. MSF (Doctors Without Borders) is treating more than 20 wounded, some with severe burns.
story.why: it is one of the deadliest single strikes of Sudan's war, which began in April 2023, and it drags a long-disputed border area, which diplomats say has become an RSF fuel route, further into the conflict.

story.headline: UN sees up to 2.8C of warming
story.summary: UNEP's Emissions Gap Report 2026 says 1.5C overshoot is now unavoidable and current policies lead to 2.8C.
story.display_body: The UN Environment Programme said on Wednesday 21 October that current policies put the world on course for up to 2.8°C of warming this century, and that overshooting the 1.5°C limit can no longer be avoided. Even if every national climate plan (NDC, a country's pledge under the Paris Agreement) is fully delivered, warming would reach 2.6°C. UNEP says both figures are worse than last year's because of the US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of past emissions, and that new pledges since then have made a "negligible" difference. The report's best case is a "lowest possible overshoot": peak warming of 1.7–1.8°C around mid-century, then a return to 1.5°C by 2100, with about a 50% chance. That would need emissions cuts of 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040 compared with 2025 levels, against the 5–8% by 2030 that today's pledges would deliver. It would also need about 320 billion tonnes of CO2 to be removed from the air over the century, which UNEP calls uncertain.
story.why: the UN's own yardstick now says the 1.5°C goal can only be met by overshooting it and coming back, which sets the terms for this year's climate summit.

story.headline: Nigeria confirms first Ebola case
story.summary: WHO says Nigeria confirmed its first Ebola Bundibugyo case, a traveller from Uganda in Abuja.
story.display_body: Nigeria has confirmed its first case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease, in a woman in Abuja who had recently travelled from Uganda, the World Health Organization said on Wednesday 21 October. She developed symptoms on 7 October, four days after arriving, went to a private clinic in Abuja on 11 October, and was confirmed by laboratory test on 20 October. She is in isolation, and 44 contacts are being monitored. Nigeria is the fifth country to detect this strain since the Democratic Republic of the Congo declared an outbreak in mid-May; Congo has recorded more than 9,500 cases and 4,200 deaths as of 18 October, its deadliest outbreak ever. There is no approved vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain.
story.why: the nine days between the clinic visit and the diagnosis is the risk, in Africa's most populous country, because it leaves time for unnoticed spread.

story.headline: French 10-year yield tops 5%
story.summary: France's 10-year borrowing rate passed 5% for the first time since 2002.
story.display_body: France's ten-year borrowing cost rose above 5% on Wednesday 21 October for the first time since 2002, Le Monde reports. The gap with Germany's benchmark rate was 1.57 percentage points, after closing at 1.53 on Tuesday, its widest since November 2011. France now pays more to borrow than Italy (4.57%) or Spain (4.06%). Le Monde links the move to investor doubts, sharpened by the violence of 17–18 October, about whether the government can deliver a 2027 budget that plans €43 billion of new savings to bring the deficit to 5% of GDP.
story.why: a higher benchmark rate raises France's debt bill and, over time, its mortgage and business-loan rates.

story.headline: Iran claims three tankers hit mines
story.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed three more tankers struck mines south of the Strait of Hormuz.
story.display_body: Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed on Tuesday 20 October that three more oil tankers had hit Guard-laid mines south of the Strait of Hormuz. In statements carried by its Sepah News site and state TV, the Guards said two "violating" ships caught fire and were immobilised on a route they call "illegal", and that a third, carrying "two million barrels" of crude with its radar switched off, exploded. No independent confirmation from shipping authorities or the owners had been found by this edition.

story.headline: Double surnames return in 2027
story.summary: The Federal Council set 1 January 2027 for married couples to take an official double surname again.
story.display_body: From Friday 1 January 2027, married couples in Switzerland can again take an official double surname, the Federal Council decided on Wednesday 21 October. Double surnames have been barred since 2013; couples could only use an unofficial hyphenated "alliance name". The new double name can be written with or without a hyphen, but it stays unavailable for children. People who are already married can declare one at their civil-registry office from January. The alliance name can still appear on passports and ID cards during a transition period whose length has not been set yet. The changes to the civil-registry ordinance are due in November.

story.headline: Short-time work crisis rules to unwind
story.summary: The Federal Council plans a staggered return to normal short-time work compensation rules.
story.display_body: The Federal Council said on Wednesday 21 October that it plans to phase out, step by step, the crisis rules for short-time work compensation (RHT/Kurzarbeit, where unemployment insurance covers wages for hours lost). Today firms can claim for up to 24 months instead of the normal 12, and pay only one waiting day instead of three. The 24-month maximum runs until 31 January 2027. In December the government will decide whether to extend it from February and how to return to 12 months during 2027. The three-day waiting period is due back from 2028, with a consultation in spring 2027. The government points to its 17 September forecast of 1.7% growth in 2026 and 1.6% in 2027.
story.why: firms still relying on short-time work lose the extended cushion gradually through 2027 rather than all at once, and the government can still pause if the outlook worsens.

story.headline: Wyssmann enters SVP Federal Council race
story.summary: Solothurn SVP national councillor Remy Wyssmann is running to succeed Guy Parmelin.
story.display_body: Solothurn SVP national councillor Rémy Wyssmann said on Wednesday 21 October that he is running to succeed Federal Councillor Guy Parmelin. The 59-year-old lawyer and notary has sat in the National Council since December 2023. He is only the second declared candidate after Geneva national councillor Céline Amaudruz, after several better-known names ruled themselves out. He said he would stand up for the middle class. The SVP parliamentary group picks its ticket on Friday 20 November, and the Federal Assembly elects on Wednesday 9 December.

story.headline: Court bars PostFinance voiceprints
story.summary: The Federal Administrative Court ruled PostFinance needs explicit consent to store callers' voiceprints.
story.display_body: The Federal Administrative Court has ruled that PostFinance may not create voiceprints of hotline callers without their explicit consent, SRF reported on Wednesday 21 October. Since autumn 2018, PostFinance's hotline recorded a voice profile of callers to recognise them next time, unless they told the agent they objected. The court agreed with the Federal Data Protection Commissioner that this opt-out is not enough: a voice reveals emotions, health and personal traits, so an opt-in is required. PostFinance must get consent for existing profiles or delete them. The ruling can be appealed to the Federal Supreme Court.
story.why: it sets a test for any Swiss company using voice biometrics for customer identification.

story.headline: Bern backs cement carbon border levy
story.summary: The Federal Council backed a bill for a carbon border charge on imported cement, with a trigger mechanism.
story.display_body: The Federal Council on Wednesday 21 October backed a National Council committee's bill for a carbon levy at the border on imported cement, but asked for a trigger mechanism because of the risks to trade. The bill responds to parliamentary initiative 21.432. It would make importers declare cement-based goods and pay a CO2 charge, matching what Swiss cement plants pay under the emissions-trading system and copying, for this one sector, the EU's carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM). Cement is the largest emitter among the Swiss plants in emissions trading.
